title: Can a fast wave pose as a slow one?
hook: Sample a wave too slowly and the dots can fit a different, slower wave.

knows: digital audio is a list of numbers
doesNotKnow: that too slow a sample rate turns a fast wave into a slower fake

misconception: Sampling a sound often enough or not, the samples always trace the original wave.
objective: The learner can say that a wave faster than half the sample rate gives the same samples as a slower wave, so audio is sampled at more than twice the highest frequency.

claims.text: A 4 Hz wave sampled 5 times a second gives the same sample points as a 1 Hz wave; a 2 Hz wave does not.
claims.source: Node: cos(2 pi * 4 * n/5) equals cos(2 pi * 1 * n/5) for n = 0..5 (difference < 1e-9); the 2 Hz and 0.5 Hz waves differ at some n. Demo.tsx draws dots from the same cosine with f and FS = 5.

claims.text: A wave faster than half the sample rate (2.5 Hz at 5 samples a second) looks like a slower wave.
claims.source: Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (Shannon 1949, 'Communication in the presence of noise'): frequencies above half the sampling rate alias to lower frequencies. Stage alias = |f - 5 round(f/5)|, node-checked for f = 3 (2 Hz) and 3.5 (1.5 Hz).

claims.text: That is why audio is sampled at more than twice its highest frequency.
claims.source: Shannon 1949 / any audio-engineering text (e.g. Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio): the sample rate must exceed twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing.

claims.text: The stage uses 5 samples per second and waves from 0.5 to 4 Hz, an idealised cosine wave, not a real recording.
claims.source: Stage constants FS = 5 and the slider range 0.5 to 4 Hz in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: A wave of 7 Hz is sampled 10 times a second. Which slower wave gives exactly the same sample points?
recall.why: 7 is above half of 10 (5), so it aliases to |7 - 10| = 3 Hz: the samples fit a 3 Hz wave exactly.
